claim: Deliberative decisions based on an accumulation of evidence over time depend on working memory.
source: Deliberative decisions based on an accumulation of evidence over time depend on working memory, and working memory has limitations, but how these limitations affect deliberative decision-making is not understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Working memory has limitations.
source: Deliberative decisions based on an accumulation of evidence over time depend on working memory, and working memory has limitations, but how these limitations affect deliberative decision-making is not understood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: How working-memory limitations affect deliberative decision-making is not understood.
source: Deliberative decisions based on an accumulation of evidence over time depend on working memory, and working memory has limitations, but how these limitations affect deliberative decision-making is not understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the study.

claim: Participants decided the average location of multiple visual targets in the study.
source: Participants decided the average location of multiple visual targets.
evidence: This describes the experimental task used in the study.

claim: The computed, continuous decision variable degraded with time and capacity.
source: This computed, continuous decision variable degraded with time and capacity in a manner that depended critically on the strategy used to form the decision variable.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: The degradation of the decision variable depended critically on the strategy used to form the decision variable.
source: This computed, continuous decision variable degraded with time and capacity in a manner that depended critically on the strategy used to form the decision variable.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data and model fits.

claim: One strategy involves computing the decision variable immediately upon observing the evidence and storing it as a single value in memory.
source: This dependence reflected whether the decision variable was computed either: (1) immediately upon observing the evidence, and thus stored as a single value in memory; or (2) at the time of the report, and thus stored as multiple values in memory.
evidence: This describes one of the two strategies identified in the study.

claim: Another strategy involves computing the decision variable at the time of the report, storing multiple values in memory.
source: This dependence reflected whether the decision variable was computed either: (1) immediately upon observing the evidence, and thus stored as a single value in memory; or (2) at the time of the report, and thus stored as multiple values in memory.
evidence: This describes the second of the two strategies identified in the study.

claim: Many perceptual, memory-based, and reward-based decisions depend on an accumulation of evidence over time.
source: Many perceptual, memory-based, and reward-based decisions depend on an accumulation of evidence over time (Brody and Hanks, 2016; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Ratcliff et al., 2016; Shadlen and Shohamy, 2016; Summerfield and Tsetsos, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Evidence accumulation can operate on timescales ranging from tens to hundreds of milliseconds for many perceptual decisions.
source: This dynamic process, which can operate on timescales ranging from tens to hundreds of milliseconds for many perceptual decisions to seconds or longer for reward-based and other decisions (Bernacchia et al., 2011; Gold and Stocker, 2017), requires working memory to maintain representations of new, incoming evidence and/or the aggregated, updating decision variable.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Evidence accumulation can operate on timescales of seconds or longer for reward-based and other decisions.
source: This dynamic process, which can operate on timescales ranging from tens to hundreds of milliseconds for many perceptual decisions to seconds or longer for reward-based and other decisions (Bernacchia et al., 2011; Gold and Stocker, 2017), requires working memory to maintain representations of new, incoming evidence and/or the aggregated, updating decision variable.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Evidence accumulation requires working memory to maintain representations of new, incoming evidence and/or the aggregated, updating decision variable.
source: This dynamic process, which can operate on timescales ranging from tens to hundreds of milliseconds for many perceptual decisions to seconds or longer for reward-based and other decisions (Bernacchia et al., 2011; Gold and Stocker, 2017), requires working memory to maintain representations of new, incoming evidence and/or the aggregated, updating decision variable.
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Working memory is constrained by capacity and temporal limitations.
source: Working memory is constrained by capacity and temporal limitations (Bastos et al., 2018; Cowan et al., 2008; Funahashi et al., 1989; Oberauer et al., 2016; Panichello et al., 2019; Ploner et al., 1998; Schneegans and Bays, 2018; White et al., 1994) that, in principle, could also constrain decision performance.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Working-memory limitations could, in principle, constrain decision performance.
source: Working memory is constrained by capacity and temporal limitations (Bastos et al., 2018; Cowan et al., 2008; Funahashi et al., 1989; Oberauer et al., 2016; Panichello et al., 2019; Ploner et al., 1998; Schneegans and Bays, 2018; White et al., 1994) that, in principle, could also constrain decision performance.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on known working-memory limitations.

claim: Several previous studies failed to identify working-memory constraints on decisions that depend on working memory.
source: Several previous studies failed to identify such constraints on decisions that depend on working memory, but those studies used tasks involving binary choices that may be relatively insensitive to known working-memory limitations (Liu et al., 2015; Waskom and Kiani, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Previous studies used tasks involving binary choices that may be relatively insensitive to known working-memory limitations.
source: Several previous studies failed to identify such constraints on decisions that depend on working memory, but those studies used tasks involving binary choices that may be relatively insensitive to known working-memory limitations (Liu et al., 2015; Waskom and Kiani, 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior studies supported by citations.

claim: It remains unclear if and how working-memory limitations affect decisions that require interpreting and storing continuously valued quantities.
source: It remains unclear if and how working-memory limitations affect decisions that require interpreting and storing continuously valued quantities whose representations are known to degrade over time (Ploner et al., 1998; Schneegans and Bays, 2018; Wei et al., 2012; White et al., 1994).
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap motivating the current study.

claim: Representations of continuously valued quantities are known to degrade over time.
source: It remains unclear if and how working-memory limitations affect decisions that require interpreting and storing continuously valued quantities whose representations are known to degrade over time (Ploner et al., 1998; Schneegans and Bays, 2018; Wei et al., 2012; White et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Participants were required to indicate a remembered spatial location informed by one or more briefly presented visual stimuli after a variable delay.
source: Specifically, we required participants to indicate a remembered spatial location that was informed by one or more briefly presented visual stimuli ('disks'; Figure 1) after a variable delay.
evidence: This describes the experimental task design, also illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The study compared effects of variable set size and delay when the remembered location corresponded to the perceived location of a specific disk identified at the time of interrogation.
source: We compared the effects of variable set size and delay when the remembered location corresponded to either: (1) the perceived location (angle) of a specific disk, identified at the time of interrogation, which is a design that has been used previously (Ploner et al., 1998; Schneegans and Bays, 2018; Wei et al., 2012; White et al., 1994); or (2) the computed mean angle of a set of multiple disks, which is a form of continuous decision variable whose sensitivity to working-memory limitations has not been examined in detail.
evidence: This describes one of the experimental conditions, with citations to similar prior designs.

claim: The study compared effects of variable set size and delay when the remembered location corresponded to the computed mean angle of a set of multiple disks.
source: We compared the effects of variable set size and delay when the remembered location corresponded to either: (1) the perceived location (angle) of a specific disk, identified at the time of interrogation, which is a design that has been used previously (Ploner et al., 1998; Schneegans and Bays, 2018; Wei et al., 2012; White et al., 1994); or (2) the computed mean angle of a set of multiple disks, which is a form of continuous decision variable whose sensitivity to working-memory limitations has not been examined in detail.
evidence: This describes the second experimental condition.

claim: The sensitivity of computed mean angles to working-memory limitations has not been examined in detail.
source: We compared the effects of variable set size and delay when the remembered location corresponded to either: (1) the perceived location (angle) of a specific disk, identified at the time of interrogation, which is a design that has been used previously (Ploner et al., 1998; Schneegans and Bays, 2018; Wei et al., 2012; White et al., 1994); or (2) the computed mean angle of a set of multiple disks, which is a form of continuous decision variable whose sensitivity to working-memory limitations has not been examined in detail.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap addressed by the study.

claim: The study examined effects of working-memory limitations on computed locations under a 'simultaneous' condition in which all disks were presented at once.
source: Additionally, we examined the effects of working-memory limitations on computed locations under two conditions that are representative of certain decision-making tasks. The first was a 'simultaneous' condition in which all disks (and thus all information) were presented at once.
evidence: This describes one of the experimental conditions.

claim: The study examined effects of working-memory limitations on computed locations under a 'sequential' condition in which one disk was presented later than the others.
source: The second was a 'sequential' condition in which one disk was presented later than the others. This condition required participants to adjust to a within-trial change of available decision-relevant information, typifying decisions that require evidence accumulation over time.
evidence: This describes the second experimental condition.

claim: The sequential condition required participants to adjust to a within-trial change of available decision-relevant information.
source: The second was a 'sequential' condition in which one disk was presented later than the others. This condition required participants to adjust to a within-trial change of available decision-relevant information, typifying decisions that require evidence accumulation over time.
evidence: This describes a feature of the sequential condition.

claim: The sequential condition typifies decisions that require evidence accumulation over time.
source: The second was a 'sequential' condition in which one disk was presented later than the others. This condition required participants to adjust to a within-trial change of available decision-relevant information, typifying decisions that require evidence accumulation over time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sequential condition's relevance.

claim: The precision of working memory for perceived spatial locations is often well described by diffusion dynamics.
source: For spatial working-memory tasks, the precision of working memory for perceived spatial locations is often well described by diffusion dynamics (Compte et al., 2000; Kilpatrick, 2018; Kilpatrick et al., 2013; Laing and Chow, 2001) that are commonly implemented in 'bump-attractor' models of working memory (Compte et al., 2000; Constantinidis et al., 2018; Laing and Chow, 2001; Riley and Constantinidis, 2016; Wei et al., 2012; Wimmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Diffusion dynamics are commonly implemented in 'bump-attractor' models of working memory.
source: For spatial working-memory tasks, the precision of working memory for perceived spatial locations is often well described by diffusion dynamics (Compte et al., 2000; Kilpatrick, 2018; Kilpatrick et al., 2013; Laing and Chow, 2001) that are commonly implemented in 'bump-attractor' models of working memory (Compte et al., 2000; Constantinidis et al., 2018; Laing and Chow, 2001; Riley and Constantinidis, 2016; Wei et al., 2012; Wimmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Most participants' behavior was well fit by one of two distinct strategies.
source: For the conditions we tested, most participants' behavior was well fit by one of two distinct strategies, each with its own constraints on decision performance based on different working-memory demands.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model fitting analysis.

claim: Each strategy has its own constraints on decision performance based on different working-memory demands.
source: For the conditions we tested, most participants' behavior was well fit by one of two distinct strategies, each with its own constraints on decision performance based on different working-memory demands.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model fitting analysis.

claim: In the Average-then-Diffuse (AtD) model, individual pieces of information are immediately combined into a single decision variable that is then stored in memory.
source: The first strategy was to compute the decision variable (mean disk angle) immediately upon observing the evidence (individual disk angles), and then store that value in working memory in a manner that, like for the memory of a single perceived angle, could be modeled as a single particle with a particular diffusion constant (Average-then-Diffuse model; AtD).
evidence: This describes the AtD model used in the study.

claim: In the AtD model, the decision variable is modeled as a single particle with a particular diffusion constant.
source: The first strategy was to compute the decision variable (mean disk angle) immediately upon observing the evidence (individual disk angles), and then store that value in working memory in a manner that, like for the memory of a single perceived angle, could be modeled as a single particle with a particular diffusion constant (Average-then-Diffuse model; AtD).
evidence: This describes the AtD model used in the study.

claim: In the Diffuse-then-Average (DtA) model, all relevant pieces of information are stored in memory and then combined only at the time of indicating the decision.
source: The second strategy was to maintain representations of all disk locations in working memory, modeled as separate diffusing particles, and then to combine them into a decision variable only at the time of the decision (Diffuse-then-Average model; DtA).
evidence: This describes the DtA model used in the study.

claim: In the DtA model, items are modeled as separate diffusing particles.
source: The second strategy was to maintain representations of all disk locations in working memory, modeled as separate diffusing particles, and then to combine them into a decision variable only at the time of the decision (Diffuse-then-Average model; DtA).
evidence: This describes the DtA model used in the study.

claim: The DtA strategy results in an effective diffusion constant for the average that is inversely related to the number of items.
source: Such a strategy results in an effective diffusion constant for the average that is inversely related to the number of items.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of the DtA model.

claim: Memory for computed mean locations degraded with increased set size and delay between presentation and report.
source: Our results show that like perceived locations, memory for computed mean locations degraded with increased set size (of relevant information), and delay between presentation and report.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: The degree of degradation of computed mean locations depended on the strategy used to compute the decision variables.
source: However, the degree of degradation depended on the strategy used to compute the decision variables, implying that multiple, strategy- and task-dependent effects of working-memory should be considered in the construction of future neural and computational models of decision-making.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data and model fits.

claim: Multiple, strategy- and task-dependent effects of working-memory should be considered in the construction of future neural and computational models of decision-making.
source: However, the degree of degradation depended on the strategy used to compute the decision variables, implying that multiple, strategy- and task-dependent effects of working-memory should be considered in the construction of future neural and computational models of decision-making.
evidence: This is an implication drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The study tested 17 participants.
source: We tested 17 participants (4 males, 12 females, 1 chose not to answer; age range=22–87 years).
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: The participant sample included 4 males, 12 females, and 1 who chose not to answer.
source: We tested 17 participants (4 males, 12 females, 1 chose not to answer; age range=22–87 years).
evidence: This describes the study sample demographics.

claim: The age range of participants was 22–87 years.
source: We tested 17 participants (4 males, 12 females, 1 chose not to answer; age range=22–87 years).
evidence: This describes the study sample demographics.

claim: The task was created with PsychoPy3.
source: The task was created with PsychoPy3 (Peirce et al., 2019) and distributed to participants via Pavlovia.org, which allowed participants to perform the task on their home computers after providing informed consent.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Participants performed the task on their home computers after providing informed consent.
source: The task was created with PsychoPy3 (Peirce et al., 2019) and distributed to participants via Pavlovia.org, which allowed participants to perform the task on their home computers after providing informed consent.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: The protocols were reviewed by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board and determined to meet eligibility criteria for IRB review exemption.
source: These protocols were reviewed by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board (IRB) and determined to meet eligibility criteria for IRB review exemption authorized by 45 CFR 46.104, category 2.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: The memory array consisted of 1, 2, or 5 colored disks sized 1.5% screen in diameter.
source: The array consisted of 1, 2, or 5 colored disks sized 1.5% screen in diameter.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli.

claim: The angular difference between any two adjacent disks was at least 6°.
source: The angular difference between any two adjacent disks was at least 6°, and between the two most distal disks was at most 60°.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli configuration.

claim: The angular difference between the two most distal disks was at most 60°.
source: The angular difference between any two adjacent disks was at least 6°, and between the two most distal disks was at most 60°.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli configuration.

claim: The disks from clockwise to counter-clockwise were always presented in the same order: green, red, blue, magenta, and yellow.
source: The disks from clockwise to counter-clockwise were always presented in the same order: green, red, blue, magenta, and yellow.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The consistent color ordering was intended to reduce errors caused by misbinding of location and color.
source: The consistent color ordering was intended to reduce errors caused by misbinding of location and color.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the experimental design choice.

claim: The memory array remained on the screen for 0.5 s.
source: The memory array remained on the screen for 0.5 s, while the annulus remained on the screen throughout the delay of 0, 1, or 6 s.
evidence: This describes the experimental timing.

claim: The delay period was 0, 1, or 6 s.
source: The memory array remained on the screen for 0.5 s, while the annulus remained on the screen throughout the delay of 0, 1, or 6 s.
evidence: This describes the experimental timing.

claim: Trials were excluded from analysis if the response was >30° from the correct angle.
source: Trials were excluded from analysis if the response was >30° from the correct angle.
evidence: This describes the data analysis criteria.

claim: On average, <10% of trials were excluded per delay condition per set size per block.
source: On average, <10% of trials were excluded per delay condition per set size per block (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the data exclusion rate, with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The difference in reports of Perceived spatial angles and the true probed location tended to be unbiased.
source: Specifically, the difference in reports of Perceived spatial angles and the true probed location (i.e., the response error) tended to be unbiased, in that the mean error across participants was not reliably different from 0 (Figure 3a, full distributions in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, individual participant mean errors in Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: The variance of Perceived spatial angle errors increased roughly linearly over time.
source: However, the variance of these errors increased roughly linearly over time (Figure 3c), like the location of a diffusing particle or bump attractor (Compte et al., 2000; Kilpatrick, 2018; Kilpatrick et al., 2013; Laing and Chow, 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to a figure and citations.

claim: The error variance in Perceived spatial angles depended systematically on set size.
source: This error variance depended systematically on set size (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The change in error variance over time for Perceived spatial angles did not depend on set size.
source: However, the change in error variance over time (slope of variance increase) did not depend on set size (ANOVA, significant effect of set size, F(2,32)=83.87, p=1.88e−13, and delay, F(2,32)=29.55, p=5.37e−08, but no significant interaction between set size and delay, F(4,64)=1.36, p=0.256).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Errors in reports of Computed spatial angles relative to true mean angles were unbiased.
source: Errors in reports of Computed (i.e., inferred mean) spatial angles relative to true mean angles showed similar trends, albeit with a much weaker dependence on the number of items. Specifically, Computed angle reports were also unbiased (mean error from the true value was not reliably different from 0; Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 3) but degraded (became more variable) with a roughly linear increase in variance over time (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Computed angle reports degraded with a roughly linear increase in variance over time.
source: Errors in reports of Computed (i.e., inferred mean) spatial angles relative to true mean angles showed similar trends, albeit with a much weaker dependence on the number of items. Specifically, Computed angle reports were also unbiased (mean error from the true value was not reliably different from 0; Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 3) but degraded (became more variable) with a roughly linear increase in variance over time (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Error variance in the report of the Computed average was higher at higher set sizes.
source: Error variance in the report of the Computed average was higher at higher set sizes (set size 5 had higher variances), but the rate of degradation in accuracy did not depend on set size (ANOVA, significant effect of set size, F(2,32)=13.53, p=5.515e−5, and delay, F(2,32)=130.79, p=4.441e−16, but not their interaction, F(4,64)=0.538, p=0.708).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: The rate of degradation in accuracy for Computed averages did not depend on set size.
source: Error variance in the report of the Computed average was higher at higher set sizes (set size 5 had higher variances), but the rate of degradation in accuracy did not depend on set size (ANOVA, significant effect of set size, F(2,32)=13.53, p=5.515e−5, and delay, F(2,32)=130.79, p=4.441e−16, but not their interaction, F(4,64)=0.538, p=0.708).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: For set size 2, equal numbers of well-fit participants were best fit by the AtD and the DtA models.
source: For set size 2, equal numbers of well-fit participants were best fit by the AtD (n=8) and the DtA (n=8), and as such neither model was significantly more likely to be a better fit across the population (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.756, Figure 6a, blue items).
evidence: This is a finding from the model fitting analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: For set size 5, more well-fit participants were better fit by the AtD than the DtA model.
source: Conversely, for set size 5, more well-fit participants were better fit by the AtD (n=12) than the DtA (n=3) model (p=0.0027; Figure 6a, green items).
evidence: This is a finding from the model fitting analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Participants who were not poorly fit at either set size were more likely to be better fit by AtD in set size 5 compared to set size 2.
source: Participants who were not poorly fit at either set size were more likely to be better fit by AtD in set size 5 compared to set size 2 (Wilcoxon signed-rank two-sided test for equal median log-likelihoods difference of fits of the two models across set sizes, p=0.029).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: These differences in strategy use did not correlate with the ages of the participants.
source: These differences in strategy use did not correlate with the ages of the participants (Pearson correlation, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, p>0.20).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Working-memory load might have affected participants' decision strategies, such that a higher load corresponded to an increased tendency to discard information about individual samples and hold only the relevant computed decision variable in memory.
source: These findings suggest that working-memory load might have affected our participants' decision strategies, such that a higher load corresponded to an increased tendency to discard information about individual samples (disk locations) and hold only the relevant computed decision variable in memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Early Perceived reports tended to be relatively unbiased.
source: Early Perceived reports tended to be relatively unbiased (two-sided t-test for H0: mean error=0, p>0.05; Figure 7a, full distributions in Figure 7—figure supplement 1; individual participant mean errors in Figure 7—figure supplement 2a-d) but became more variable over time in a roughly linear manner (Figure 7d), consistent with the predictions of the particle-diffusion models.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Early Perceived reports became more variable over time in a roughly linear manner.
source: Early Perceived reports tended to be relatively unbiased (two-sided t-test for H0: mean error=0, p>0.05; Figure 7a, full distributions in Figure 7—figure supplement 1; individual participant mean errors in Figure 7—figure supplement 2a-d) but became more variable over time in a roughly linear manner (Figure 7d), consistent with the predictions of the particle-diffusion models.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: For Early Perceived reports, errors were more variable at higher set sizes.
source: For higher set sizes, errors were more variable than at lower set sizes.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: For Early Perceived reports, the rate of variance increase over time did not depend on set size.
source: The rate of variance increase over time did not depend on set size (ANOVA, significant effect of set size, F(2,32)=33.44, p=1.45e−08, and delay, F(1,16)=77.02, p=1.64e−07, but not their interaction, F(2,32)=0.15, p=0.256).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Late Perceived reports were unbiased.
source: Late Perceived reports were likewise unbiased (mean error not significantly different from 0; Figure 7b, full distributions in Figure 7—figure supplement 1; individual participant mean errors in Figure 7—figure supplement 2e-h) and degraded in precision (i.e., increased in variance) over time (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Late Perceived reports degraded in precision over time.
source: Late Perceived reports were likewise unbiased (mean error not significantly different from 0; Figure 7b, full distributions in Figure 7—figure supplement 1; individual participant mean errors in Figure 7—figure supplement 2e-h) and degraded in precision (i.e., increased in variance) over time (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The degradation of Late Perceived reports did not depend on set size.
source: However, this degradation did not depend on set size (ANOVA, significant effect of delay, F(1,16)=39.28, p=1.12e−05, but not set size, F(1,16)=0.90, p=0.36 or their interaction, F(1,16)=0.0029, p=0.96).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Computed reports that required integrating both Early and Late items tended to be slightly biased towards the Early items for set size 2.
source: Conversely, Computed (i.e., inferred mean) reports that required integrating both Early and Late items tended to be slightly biased towards the Early items for set size 2 (mean=13% of the distance between the two disks closer to the Early point than a true mean; Student's two-sided t-test, p<0.001) but not set size 5 (mean=3.5% closer to the mean of N–1 items than the true mean of all items; p>0.5; Figure 7c, full distributions in Figure 7—figure supplement 1; individual participant mean errors in Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Computed reports for set size 5 were not significantly biased towards the Early items.
source: Conversely, Computed (i.e., inferred mean) reports that required integrating both Early and Late items tended to be slightly biased towards the Early items for set size 2 (mean=13% of the distance between the two disks closer to the Early point than a true mean; Student's two-sided t-test, p<0.001) but not set size 5 (mean=3.5% closer to the mean of N–1 items than the true mean of all items; p>0.5; Figure 7c, full distributions in Figure 7—figure supplement 1; individual participant mean errors in Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: The Computed report errors increased in variance over time.
source: The Computed report errors also increased in variance over time (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The overall errors of bias and variance in Computed reports did not change dramatically with training.
source: These overall errors of bias and variance did not change dramatically with training (t-tests for differences in mean and standard deviation of report errors between the first and second half of trials=0, p>0.05 in all cases).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: The magnitude of the errors of variance in Computed reports, and their change over time, depended systematically on the number of items to remember.
source: However, the magnitude of the errors of variance, and their change over time, depended systematically on the number of items to remember, such that more items corresponded to a slightly greater overall variance in reports at short delays, but less gain in variance over time (ANOVA, significant effect of set size, F(2,32)=7.73, p=1.8e−3, delay, F(1,16)=73.76, p=2.18e−07, and their interaction, F(2,32)=6.81, p=3.4e−3).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: More items corresponded to a slightly greater overall variance in Computed reports at short delays, but less gain in variance over time.
source: However, the magnitude of the errors of variance, and their change over time, depended systematically on the number of items to remember, such that more items corresponded to a slightly greater overall variance in reports at short delays, but less gain in variance over time (ANOVA, significant effect of set size, F(2,32)=7.73, p=1.8e−3, delay, F(1,16)=73.76, p=2.18e−07, and their interaction, F(2,32)=6.81, p=3.4e−3).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: The interaction of delay and set size in Computed reports suggests the representation of the Computed value diffused in working memory with a different diffusion constant than for a single Perceived value.
source: This interaction of delay and set size suggests the representation of the Computed value diffused in working memory with a different diffusion constant than for a single Perceived value.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical findings.

claim: For Sequential set size 2, 9 participants were best fit by the AtD model and 8 by the DtA model.
source: In general, both strategies were used by our participants in each of the two set-size conditions (for set sizes 2, 9, and 8 participants were best fit by the AtD and DtA models, respectively; for set size, 5, 8, and 8 participants were best fit by the AtD and DtA models, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the model fitting analysis.

claim: For Sequential set size 5, 8 participants were best fit by the AtD model and 8 by the DtA model.
source: In general, both strategies were used by our participants in each of the two set-size conditions (for set sizes 2, 9, and 8 participants were best fit by the AtD and DtA models, respectively; for set size, 5, 8, and 8 participants were best fit by the AtD and DtA models, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the model fitting analysis.

claim: For Sequential set size 2, neither model was significantly more likely to be a better fit across the population.
source: For set size 2, one more participant was best fit by the AtD (n=9) versus the DtA (n=8) model (Wilcoxon signed-rank two-sided test for the median difference in the log-likelihoods of fits of the two models to data from each participant=0, p=0.868).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: For Sequential set size 5, neither model was significantly more likely to be a better fit across the population.
source: For set size 5, two more participants were best fit by the AtD (n=9) versus the DtA (n=7) model (p=0.234).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Participants well fit at either Sequential set size were not significantly more likely to be fit by either model across set sizes.
source: Participants well fit at either set size were not significantly more likely to be fit by either model across set sizes (Wilcoxon signed-rank two-sided test for identical median log-likelihoods difference of fits of the two models across set size, p=0.283).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Differences in strategy use in Sequential conditions did not correlate with age of participants.
source: These differences in strategy use did not correlate with age of participants (Figure 10—figure supplement 1, Pearson correlation, p>0.20).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: On average, participants lost fidelity in their representations of a Computed value when it needed to be computed from sequentially presented information.
source: Thus, on average, participants lost fidelity in their representations of a Computed value when it needed to be computed from sequentially presented information, as in many processes of evidence accumulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The dynamics of degradation differed for the two strategies in Sequential conditions.
source: The dynamics of this degradation differed for the two strategies, neither of which was statistically more likely than the other across our participants.
evidence: This is a finding from the model fitting analysis.

claim: Three participants previously identified as AtD and three participants previously identified as DtA were slightly better described by a hybrid model for Sequential set size 5.
source: We found that three participants previously identified as AtD and three participants previously identified as DtA were slightly better described by the hybrid model (average LL difference for formerly DtA participants=0.34, average difference from formerly AtD participants 1.28).
evidence: This is a finding from the alternative model fitting analysis.

claim: People likely use a spectrum of strategies, including nuanced combinations of AtD-like and DtA-like dynamics.
source: This finding is consistent with the idea that people likely use a spectrum of strategies, including nuanced combinations of AtD-like and DtA-like dynamics (which were the focus of the present study, to demonstrate how those dynamics can give rise to identifiable signatures of behavioral errors) that warrant further consideration when building more detailed models of memory-dependent decision-making.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The use of different strategies did not appear to reflect a tendency of individual participants to use a particular strategy across different conditions.
source: The use of different strategies (i.e., those captured by the AtD and DtA models) did not appear to reflect a tendency of individual participants to use a particular strategy across different conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Strategy use in set size 2 Simultaneous was not predictive of use in set size 5 Simultaneous.
source: We failed to reject the null hypothesis that there is no relationship between a participant's strategy use across set size for both Simultaneous and Sequential conditions (i.e., strategy use in set size 2 Simultaneous was not predictive of use in set size 5 Simultaneous, nor was it for Sequential conditions; p=0.31 and p=1, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Strategy use in set size 2 Sequential was not predictive of use in set size 5 Sequential.
source: We failed to reject the null hypothesis that there is no relationship between a participant's strategy use across set size for both Simultaneous and Sequential conditions (i.e., strategy use in set size 2 Simultaneous was not predictive of use in set size 5 Simultaneous, nor was it for Sequential conditions; p=0.31 and p=1, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Strategy use across temporal conditions for set size 2 was not predictive.
source: We also failed to reject the null hypothesis that there is no relationship between a participant's strategy use across temporal conditions for both set sizes 2 and 5 (p=0.54 and p=1, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Strategy use across temporal conditions for set size 5 was not predictive.
source: We also failed to reject the null hypothesis that there is no relationship between a participant's strategy use across temporal conditions for both set sizes 2 and 5 (p=0.54 and p=1, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Only under set size 5 Simultaneous conditions were participants more likely to use one strategy (AtD) over the other (DtA).
source: Thus, we found that only under set size 5 were Simultaneous conditions participants more likely to use one strategy (AtD) over the other (DtA).
evidence: This is a summary finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: In all other tested cases, participants were equally likely to use either strategy.
source: In all other tested cases, participants were equally likely to use either strategy, and strategy use was not predictive across conditions for individual participants.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Strategy use was not predictive across conditions for individual participants.
source: In all other tested cases, participants were equally likely to use either strategy, and strategy use was not predictive across conditions for individual participants.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Computed variables based on either simultaneously or sequentially presented information were susceptible to the same kinds of working-memory constraints as perceived variables.
source: Our primary finding was that computed variables based on either simultaneously or sequentially presented information were susceptible to the same kinds of working-memory constraints as perceived variables.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study.

claim: Working-memory limitations corresponded to a decrease in precision over time for computed variables.
source: These working-memory limitations corresponded to a decrease in precision over time, which places critical constraints on the kinds of decision variables that are required to persist over time, such as when decisions are delayed.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study.

claim: The variability caused by singular events such as sensory encoding or averaging tended to be ~10° in Simultaneous conditions.
source: Specifically, the variability caused by singular events such as sensory encoding or averaging tended to be ~10° in Simultaneous conditions, whereas noise accumulating during memory delay periods was typically ~3.5°/s.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Noise accumulating during memory delay periods was typically ~3.5°/s.
source: Specifically, the variability caused by singular events such as sensory encoding or averaging tended to be ~10° in Simultaneous conditions, whereas noise accumulating during memory delay periods was typically ~3.5°/s.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: After ~3 s, the noise that can be attributed to memory versus non-memory sources is about equal.
source: Therefore, after ~3 s, the noise that can be attributed to memory versus non-memory sources is about equal, and after this point memory noise begins to dominate overall variability.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the quantitative findings.

claim: After ~3 s, memory noise begins to dominate overall variability.
source: Therefore, after ~3 s, the noise that can be attributed to memory versus non-memory sources is about equal, and after this point memory noise begins to dominate overall variability.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the quantitative findings.

claim: Previous studies found no effect of extra delays on the effectiveness of evidence accumulation for certain decisions.
source: This result appears to contradict previous findings that found no effect of extra delays on the effectiveness of evidence accumulation for certain decisions (Liu et al., 2015; Waskom and Kiani, 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies used tasks with binary choices that required decision variables with less clear sensitivity to the kinds of working-memory effects found in the current study.
source: However, those studies used tasks with binary choices that required decision variables with less clear sensitivity to the kinds of working-memory effects we found in the context of a continuous, spatially based decision variable.
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior studies to explain the apparent contradiction.

claim: Increasing the number of decision-relevant items decreased the accuracy of the continuous decision variable.
source: Additionally, we found that increasing the number of decision-relevant items also decreased the accuracy of the continuous decision variable, although the nature of this effect was variable.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: The nature of the effect of increasing decision-relevant items on accuracy was variable.
source: Additionally, we found that increasing the number of decision-relevant items also decreased the accuracy of the continuous decision variable, although the nature of this effect was variable.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: More work is needed to fully characterize the conditions under which temporal and capacity limitations on the precision of working-memory representations affect decisions based on those representations.
source: More work is needed to fully characterize the conditions under which temporal and capacity limitations on the precision of working-memory representations affect decisions based on those representations.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The AtD model stipulates that a participant first calculates and then stores the Computed value.
source: The first strategy, captured by the AtD model, stipulated that a participant first calculates and then stores the Computed value.
evidence: This describes the AtD model.

claim: The AtD model's key prediction is that a Computed value should be susceptible to the same effects of working-memory limitations as a single remembered Perceptual value in simultaneous conditions.
source: Its key prediction is that a Computed value should be susceptible to the same effects of working-memory limitations as a single remembered Perceptual value in simultaneous conditions.
evidence: This describes a key prediction of the AtD model.

claim: The DtA model stipulates that all individual values are stored in working memory until the time of decision.
source: The second strategy, captured by the DtA model, stipulated that all individual values are stored in working memory until the time of decision.
evidence: This describes the DtA model.

claim: The DtA model's key prediction is that the overall rate of variance increase is inversely related to the number of items.
source: Its key prediction is that the overall rate of variance increase is inversely related to the number of items.
evidence: This describes a key prediction of the DtA model.

claim: The differences in performance of adopters of each of the strategies were often minimal in the present study.
source: Although the differences in performance of adopters of each of the strategies were often minimal in the present study, the differences in strategy rely on rates of degradation over time and thus performance differences would be expected to grow over longer delays.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Performance differences between strategies would be expected to grow over longer delays.
source: Although the differences in performance of adopters of each of the strategies were often minimal in the present study, the differences in strategy rely on rates of degradation over time and thus performance differences would be expected to grow over longer delays.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model properties.

claim: Participants tended to use an AtD strategy for the Simultaneous conditions with a relatively high load (five items).
source: We found that participants tended to use an AtD strategy for the Simultaneous conditions with a relatively high load (five items), but otherwise were roughly equally likely to use either strategy, including for all Sequential conditions.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the model fitting analysis.

claim: Participants were roughly equally likely to use either strategy for Simultaneous conditions with lower loads and for all Sequential conditions.
source: We found that participants tended to use an AtD strategy for the Simultaneous conditions with a relatively high load (five items), but otherwise were roughly equally likely to use either strategy, including for all Sequential conditions.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the model fitting analysis.

claim: Several individuals switched from using DtA for the smaller set size to AtD for the larger set size in the Simultaneous condition.
source: For example, we found that for the Simultaneous condition, several individuals switched from using DtA for the smaller set size to AtD for the larger set size, but we do not know if this switch was a consequence of their personal working-memory capacities.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: It is not known if the switch from DtA to AtD with increasing set size was a consequence of participants' personal working-memory capacities.
source: For example, we found that for the Simultaneous condition, several individuals switched from using DtA for the smaller set size to AtD for the larger set size, but we do not know if this switch was a consequence of their personal working-memory capacities.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of the current study.

claim: From an optimality standpoint, DtA better preserves a computed value compared to AtD for a given level of non-time-dependent noise and cost per storage item (A), but only if A remains low (<1).
source: From an optimality standpoint, DtA better preserves a computed value compared to AtD for a given level of non-time-dependent noise and cost per storage item (A), but only if A remains low (<1).
evidence: This is an inference from the model properties.

claim: It would be interesting to see if for more intermediate set sizes there is a reliable increase in the probability of a participant using AtD with a progression that relates to other measures of the individual's working-memory capacity.
source: It would be interesting to see if for more intermediate set sizes (i.e., three or four items) there is a reliable increase in the probability of a participant using AtD with a progression that relates to other measures of the individual's working-memory capacity.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Future studies could provide more detailed instructions, incentives, and/or feedback to better understand the flexibility with which different strategies can be employed.
source: Future studies could provide more detailed instructions, incentives, and/or feedback to better understand the flexibility with which these different strategies can be employed.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The study did not consider possible differences in metabolic energy and other resources needed to implement the different working-memory demands of different strategies.
source: First, we did not consider possible differences in metabolic energy and other resources needed to implement the different working-memory demands of different strategies (van den Berg and Ma, 2018).
evidence: This identifies a limitation of the current study, with a citation.

claim: Future studies of strategy heterogeneity may need to consider how different strategies minimize both response errors and execution costs.
source: Future studies of strategy heterogeneity may need to consider how different strategies minimize both response errors and execution costs.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The DtA model assumed no interference between multiple items stored in memory.
source: Second, our DtA model assumed no interference between multiple items stored in memory.
evidence: This describes an assumption of the DtA model.

claim: The assumption of no interference between multiple items stored in memory is undoubtedly an oversimplification.
source: This assumption is undoubtedly an oversimplification, given that storage of multiple items has been both hypothesized and shown to create attraction and repulsion (Almeida et al., 2015; Krishnan et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a model limitation, supported by citations.

claim: Storage of multiple items has been both hypothesized and shown to create attraction and repulsion.
source: This assumption is undoubtedly an oversimplification, given that storage of multiple items has been both hypothesized and shown to create attraction and repulsion (Almeida et al., 2015; Krishnan et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Directional drift can create a decrease in variance over time that could affect decision variables that involve multiple quantities stored at once.
source: Such directional drift can create a decrease in variance over time that could affect decision variables that involve multiple quantities stored at once.
evidence: This is an inference about potential effects not captured by the current models.

claim: The DtA model assumed that each item was stored individually.
source: Third, our DtA model also assumed that each item was stored individually.
evidence: This describes an assumption of the DtA model.

claim: Items could have been discarded or merged (chunked), leading to different memory loads which could also affect performance.
source: Alternatively, items could have been discarded or merged (chunked) (Krishnan et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2012), leading to different memory loads which could also affect performance.
evidence: This is an alternative possibility not captured by the current models, supported by citations.

claim: Most participants used strategies that were well described by the AtD or DtA model.
source: Fourth, most of our participants used strategies that were well described by the AtD or DtA model.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the model fitting analysis.

claim: Under certain conditions (Sequential, set size 5) some participants seemed to use hybrid strategies.
source: However, under certain conditions (i.e., Sequential, set size 5) some participants seemed to use hybrid strategies.
evidence: This is a finding from the alternative model fitting analysis.

claim: Hybrid strategies would suggest extensive flexibility in when and how evidence is incorporated into computed decision variables.
source: This kind of strategy would suggest extensive flexibility in when and how evidence is incorporated into computed decision variables, thereby placing potentially complex demands on working memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hybrid strategy finding.

claim: Both primary models were based on assumptions of a drifting memory representation.
source: Both of our primary models were based on assumptions of a drifting memory representation.
evidence: This describes a fundamental assumption of the models.

claim: Random drift is traditionally associated with attractor models of working memory.
source: This random drift is traditionally associated with attractor models of working memory (Bays, 2014; Compte et al., 2000; Macoveanu et al., 2007; Wei et al., 2012) that have been used extensively to describe the underlying neural mechanisms (Funahashi et al., 1989; Shafi et al., 2007; Takeda and Funahashi, 2002; Wimmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Attractor models of working memory have been used extensively to describe the underlying neural mechanisms.
source: This random drift is traditionally associated with attractor models of working memory (Bays, 2014; Compte et al., 2000; Macoveanu et al., 2007; Wei et al., 2012) that have been used extensively to describe the underlying neural mechanisms (Funahashi et al., 1989; Shafi et al., 2007; Takeda and Funahashi, 2002; Wimmer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In attractor models, neural network activity is induced by an external stimulus and then maintained via excitatory connections of similarly tuned neurons and long-ranged inhibition.
source: In these models, neural network activity is induced by an external stimulus and then maintained via excitatory connections of similarly tuned neurons and long-ranged inhibition.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of attractor models.

claim: In attractor models, random noise causes the center of activity to drift in a manner that can depend on the delay duration, set size, and/or their interaction.
source: Random noise causes the center of this activity (which represents the stimulus) to drift in a manner that, dependent on the implementation, can depend on the delay duration, set size, and/or their interaction (Almeida et al., 2015; Bays, 2014; Koyluoglu et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of attractor models, supported by citations.

claim: A recent implementation of attractor models can naturally compute a running average based on sequentially presented information.
source: A recent implementation even can naturally compute a running average based on sequentially presented information (Esnaola-Acebes et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent literature.

claim: The study's results imply that attractor models should be extended to support the flexible use of different strategies that govern when and how incoming information is used to form averages.
source: Our results imply that such models should be extended to support the flexible use of different strategies that govern when and how incoming information is used to form such averages.
evidence: This is an implication drawn from the study's findings.

claim: It will be interesting to see if a flexible model can account for neural activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
source: It will be interesting to see if such a flexible model can account for neural activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which includes neurons with persistent activity that has been associated with both spatial working memory (Compte et al., 2000; Constantinidis et al., 2018; Riley and Constantinidis, 2016; Wei et al., 2012; Wimmer et al., 2014) and the formation of decisions based on an accumulation of evidence (Curtis and D'Esposito, 2003; Heekeren et al., 2006; Heekeren et al., 2008; Kim and Shadlen, 1999; Lin et al., 2020; Philiastides et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research, supported by citations.

claim: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex includes neurons with persistent activity that has been associated with both spatial working memory and the formation of decisions based on an accumulation of evidence.
source: It will be interesting to see if such a flexible model can account for neural activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which includes neurons with persistent activity that has been associated with both spatial working memory (Compte et al., 2000; Constantinidis et al., 2018; Riley and Constantinidis, 2016; Wei et al., 2012; Wimmer et al., 2014) and the formation of decisions based on an accumulation of evidence (Curtis and D'Esposito, 2003; Heekeren et al., 2006; Heekeren et al., 2008; Kim and Shadlen, 1999; Lin et al., 2020; Philiastides et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Participant accuracy for both perceived and computed values was subject to working-memory limitations of both time and capacity in this spatial, continuous task.
source: In conclusion, we found that in this spatial, continuous task, participant accuracy for both perceived and computed values was subject to working-memory limitations of both time and capacity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: Behavior was consistent with both storage strategies investigated in the study.
source: Additionally, we found behavior that was consistent with both the storage strategies we investigated.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: Different participants employed different strategies for storing a computed value.
source: The fact that different participants employed different strategies for storing a computed value (such as a decision variable) and that these strategies have different consequences on overall accuracy has important implications for not only future neural network models of working memory, but also for future computational models of decision-making.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: Different strategies have different consequences on overall accuracy.
source: The fact that different participants employed different strategies for storing a computed value (such as a decision variable) and that these strategies have different consequences on overall accuracy has important implications for not only future neural network models of working memory, but also for future computational models of decision-making.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: The finding that different participants employed different strategies with different consequences on accuracy has important implications for future neural network models of working memory.
source: The fact that different participants employed different strategies for storing a computed value (such as a decision variable) and that these strategies have different consequences on overall accuracy has important implications for not only future neural network models of working memory, but also for future computational models of decision-making.
evidence: This is an implication drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The finding that different participants employed different strategies with different consequences on accuracy has important implications for future computational models of decision-making.
source: The fact that different participants employed different strategies for storing a computed value (such as a decision variable) and that these strategies have different consequences on overall accuracy has important implications for not only future neural network models of working memory, but also for future computational models of decision-making.
